title: What the Fossil Record Cannot Say
standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The fossil record is the primary evidence for the history of life, and it is a sample rather than a census. Understanding what it can establish requires understanding, first, what had to happen for anything to be in it at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: An organism becomes a fossil only under a narrow set of conditions. It has to be buried quickly, in sediment, in a place where the sediment will survive, and it has to have parts durable enough to persist while the surrounding material turns to rock.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each of those conditions filters. Hard parts survive and soft ones rarely do, so a world of worms and jellyfish leaves almost nothing, and the apparent abundance of shelled animals in the record is partly a fact about shells.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Environment filters as well. Sediment accumulates in river deltas, lake beds and shallow seas, and an animal that lived on a mountainside is in a place that erodes rather than accumulates, so entire habitats are nearly absent.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This produces a specific and well-known trap. The last fossil of a species is almost never the last individual, because rarity precedes extinction and a rare animal is unlikely to be preserved, so the record consistently makes extinctions look earlier and more abrupt than they were.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What palaeontologists do about this is instructive. A date for an extinction is published with a range rather than a point, and that range is calculated from how often the species appears in the layers below, which converts an unknown into a stated uncertainty.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Some questions remain genuinely open and are marked as such in the literature. Whether a particular lineage declined over a million years or vanished in a decade is frequently not resolvable with the material available, and the honest papers say which of those they cannot distinguish.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the record supports two kinds of statement with very different strength. That an organism existed at a time and place is as firm as evidence gets, because the specimen is physical. That something did not exist is an inference from absence, and its strength depends entirely on how thoroughly the relevant rocks have been searched.

title: How Confident Is a Climate Projection
standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: An assessment report on climate runs to thousands of pages and is summarised in a few. The summaries are what circulate, and the thing most frequently lost in the compression is the vocabulary the report uses to say how sure it is.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That vocabulary is defined rather than conversational. Terms such as virtually certain, very likely, likely and about as likely as not each correspond to a stated probability range, and the definitions are printed in the report so that a reader can convert a word into a number.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Likely, for instance, means at least a two in three chance. A reader who takes it in its ordinary sense, as meaning probably or expected, has read a hedge as a prediction, and the report has done what it could to prevent that.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A second scale operates alongside the first and is often confused with it. Confidence describes how good the underlying evidence is, and a finding can be assigned high confidence and a wide probability range at the same time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Those two are genuinely independent. High confidence that a quantity lies somewhere in a broad range is a coherent position, and so is low confidence about a narrow one, and a summary that reports only the number has dropped the half that says how much to trust it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The reports also distinguish between what is being projected. Physical quantities such as warming under a stated emissions scenario are treated differently from consequences that depend on how societies respond, and the second carry wider ranges for reasons that are not about physics.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Where the science does not support a statement, the reports say so in the same formal register. Phrases marking limited evidence or low agreement appear throughout, and they are statements about the literature rather than about the world.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the uncertainty is not a weakness the documents are admitting. It is the most carefully constructed part of them, built to let a reader distinguish a well-constrained finding from a poorly constrained one, and it is the first thing a short summary removes.

note: Hand out the definitions table and a news article about the same report. The exercise is to restore the calibrated word the coverage replaced.

title: The Numbers We Do Not Have
standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Quantitative history depends on records that were created for other purposes, and for most of the past the records needed to answer a modern question simply do not exist.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Population before the first census is the clearest case. Estimates for a medieval or ancient population are built from proxies: hearth counts made for taxation, numbers of households in a survey, the carrying capacity of farmland, the size of a city's walls.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each proxy requires a conversion factor that cannot be measured. Turning hearths into people requires an assumed household size, and historians who prefer four and a half rather than five are producing estimates that differ by about ten per cent before any other disagreement.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The conversions compound. An estimate built from three assumptions each uncertain by twenty per cent can be out by far more than twenty per cent, and a figure stated to three significant figures hides that it rests on a chain of judgements.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The surviving records are also not a random sample of the records that were made. Documents survive where institutions were stable, where the climate was dry and where nobody had a reason to destroy them, which means survival correlates with exactly the conditions a historian might want to study. A region that was invaded repeatedly is underrepresented in the evidence about invasion.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Good practice addresses this by stating ranges and assumptions rather than figures. A paper giving a population as between nine and fourteen million, with the conversion factor named, has told a reader what the uncertainty consists of.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The practice that causes damage is the restatement. A range published carefully becomes a midpoint in a later survey, the midpoint becomes a figure in a textbook, and the figure is then cited as though it were counted.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the thorough use of this evidence requires two separate judgements. One is what the figures suggest, and the other is how far back the chain of restatement goes before a reader reaches somebody who stated a range and said what was in it.

questions.a: Turning hearth counts into people requires it, and historians preferring four and a half rather than five produce estimates differing by about ten per cent before any other disagreement.

Summarize the problem with historical population figures.
questions.a: Estimates rest on proxies such as hearth counts, each needing an unmeasurable conversion factor, and the uncertainties compound so a precise-looking figure hides a chain of judgements. Surviving records favour stable institutions and dry climates, good practice states ranges with assumptions named, and restatement turns a careful range into a midpoint and then into a cited figure.

proxy: a measurable thing standing in for one that cannot be measured directly, such as hearths for people.
conversion factor: the assumed ratio used to turn a proxy into the quantity wanted.
Describe the connection between restatement and a reader's confidence.
questions.a: A range published carefully becomes a midpoint, then a textbook figure cited as though it were counted, so a reader must ask how far back the chain goes before someone stated a range.

note: Pairs with grade 9's Domesday article. That one asked what a source was built to capture, and this asks what happens to an estimate as it is repeated.

title: What the Unemployment Rate Leaves Out
standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The unemployment rate is among the most widely reported economic figures, and almost nobody who quotes it could state its definition. It is not the proportion of adults without a job, and the difference between those two quantities is large.

paras.label: B
paras.text: To be counted as unemployed under the standard definition, a person must be without work, available to start, and have actively looked for work in a recent period, usually the last four weeks.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each of those conditions excludes people. Somebody who stopped looking because they believed no suitable work existed satisfies the first two and fails the third, and the statistics move them out of the labour force entirely rather than counting them as unemployed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: This produces a counterintuitive and perfectly routine result. When conditions worsen enough that people stop searching, the measured unemployment rate can fall, and the fall is real within the definition and misleading outside it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The part-time condition is treated differently again. Someone working four hours a week who wants full-time work is employed under the headline measure, so a shift from full employment to insufficient employment may not register in the figure at all. An economy in which hours collapse and nobody is dismissed can show a stable rate throughout.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The statistical agencies know all of this and publish more than one measure, in the same release and on the same day. A broader series includes discouraged workers and those working part-time for economic reasons, and it is available at the same moment as the headline and is reported far less often by anybody.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The headline measure is not a worse measure, and it is not an attempt to flatter anybody. A single number has to draw a boundary somewhere, and this boundary is internationally comparable and consistent over time, which the broader one is less able to be.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What follows is a specific reading discipline. The figure answers a precisely defined question, and whether that question is the one a reader has is a separate matter which the number itself does not raise and does not settle.

questions.a: Being without work, being available to start, and having actively looked for work in a recent period, usually the last four weeks.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why the rate can fall as conditions worsen) and paragraph G (i.e. why the headline measure is not worse).

questions.a: It counts people without work who are available and actively searching, so those who stopped looking leave the labour force rather than being counted, which can make the rate fall as conditions worsen. Part-time workers wanting full-time work count as employed, broader measures exist and are reported less, and the headline is defined for international comparability rather than to flatter.

questions.q:
labour force: those employed plus those actively seeking work, which excludes people who have stopped looking.
discouraged worker: someone who wants work and has stopped searching because they believe none is available.
Describe the connection between the definition's boundary and what a reader should ask.
questions.a: The figure answers a precisely defined question, so a reader must separately ask whether that is the question they have, which the number does not raise or settle.

note: Pairs with grade 8's census article and grade 9's index article. Three grades of the same idea: a measure is a decision about what counts.

title: The Limits of a Genetic Ancestry Test
standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A commercial ancestry test returns percentages: a figure for each of several regions, summing to a hundred. The precision of the presentation is considerably greater than the precision of the method, and the two are rarely distinguished in the accompanying material.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The underlying measurement is real and is of a specific kind. The test reads variants at a large number of positions in a person's genome, and those readings are accurate.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What happens next is comparison. The pattern of variants is compared against reference panels: groups of people from particular places whose genomes have been sequenced and who are treated as representing the ancestry of those places.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The reference panels are where the uncertainty concentrates. They are samples, of unequal size, from populations defined by present-day geography, and the assumption that living people in a region represent the people who lived there several centuries ago is an assumption rather than a finding.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This is why results change without any new sample. A company that expands or revises its panels issues updated percentages to existing customers, and a person whose figure for one region moves by ten points has not changed; the comparison set has.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The method also has very different power at different depths. Identifying a close biological relative is extremely reliable, because shared segments of chromosome are long and unmistakable, and that is a different operation from estimating a continental percentage. The same test performs both and reports them in the same place.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is a further limit that no improvement in method will ever remove, because it is a property of inheritance rather than of measurement. A person inherits half their genome from each parent, and the half that is passed on is a random selection, so an ancestor eight generations back may have contributed nothing detectable to a living descendant.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What the test establishes firmly is therefore narrower than what it reports. Close relationships are near-certain, broad patterns are informative, and a specific percentage for a specific region is an estimate against a changing reference whose uncertainty the figure does not display.

note: The firm claim and the soft one are produced by the same instrument and reported in the same document. Ask students to separate them without dismissing either.

title: Why Cities Are Hotter
standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A city is measurably warmer than the countryside around it, by several degrees on a still night, and the difference is produced by a short list of physical causes that have nothing to do with the climate as a whole.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is absorption. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofing take in more of the sun's energy than vegetation or pale ground, and the difference in reflectivity between a tree canopy and a car park is substantial.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is storage. Concrete, brick and stone hold heat through the day and release it slowly after sunset, which is why the difference between a city and its surroundings is largest at night rather than at noon.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is the absence of water. A leaf cools its surroundings by evaporating water, and a surface that sheds rain into a drain within minutes performs none of that cooling, so paving a surface removes an air conditioner nobody had installed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A fourth is geometry, and it is the least obvious of the four. Streets lined with tall buildings trap radiation between their walls, re-reflecting it from one face to another rather than letting it escape upward to the sky, and a narrow street with high sides on both of them cools far more slowly after dark than an open field does.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So far this is physics, and the second idea begins where the physics stops. The heat is not distributed evenly across a city, and the pattern it forms is not random.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Tree cover, park provision and the proportion of a neighbourhood under paving vary enormously within a single city, and in many cities those variations track decades of decisions about where to invest, which roads to widen and which districts to clear.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The two ideas produce something neither contains alone. The physics explains why a surface is hot, the history explains why that surface is in one neighbourhood rather than another, and a heat map of a city is simultaneously a record of materials and a record of spending.

title: Where a Prisoner Counts
standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A census records where people are, and that sounds like a factual question with a factual answer. For a person in prison it is not, because the place they are and the place they belong to are different, and a rule has to choose.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Most census practice counts a person at their usual residence, defined as where they live and sleep most of the time. Applied to a prison, that rule counts an incarcerated person as a resident of the town containing the facility.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The consequence appears when districts are drawn, which is where a count stops being a description and becomes an allocation. Legislative districts are required to contain roughly equal populations, so a district containing a large prison reaches the required number with fewer residents who are able to vote in it than a district without one.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Prisons are not distributed randomly across a country, and neither are the people in them. They are disproportionately built in rural areas with small populations and few other employers, and the people held in them come disproportionately from urban areas a considerable distance away.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the arrangement transfers representation geographically. The district with the prison gains population for the purpose of drawing boundaries, and the districts the incarcerated people came from lose it, and neither transfer involved anybody moving in any ordinary sense.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The second idea is about what a count is for, and it is where the question stops being arithmetic. A census serves several purposes at once: representation, the distribution of funds, and planning for services.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Those purposes pull in different directions here. Services in the prison town genuinely are used by the people in the facility, so counting them there is right for planning, and representation is arguably owed to the community a person will return to.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The two ideas together make the problem clear in a way neither does separately. There is no single correct place to count a person, because the count is doing several jobs, and the same figure cannot be correct for all of them at once.

title: The Grid and the Weather
standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: An electricity grid has a property that distinguishes it from almost every other network. Supply and demand have to match continuously, within a fraction of a second, because electricity is consumed at the moment it is generated.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That requirement has shaped every grid ever built. Generation is adjusted constantly to follow demand, and the ability to adjust is itself the valuable thing, which is why a plant that can increase output within minutes has historically commanded a premium over one that cannot.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Wind and solar generation change the problem rather than making it harder in a simple sense. Their output varies with weather rather than with instruction, so matching has to be achieved by moving everything else around a quantity that cannot be dispatched.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Forecasting therefore becomes part of the grid. A wind forecast accurate to a few hours ahead is now a component of system operation in the same way a power station is, and an improvement in meteorology is an improvement in grid capacity.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Storage changes the shape of the problem again. A battery converts a quantity that must be used now into one that can be used later, which turns an intermittent source into something closer to a dispatchable one, at a cost and with losses.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The second idea concerns a property of the old system that was never priced. Large spinning generators store energy in their own rotation, and that rotating mass resists sudden changes in frequency, giving operators seconds to respond to a fault.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Solar panels and most wind turbines do not provide that automatically, because they connect through electronics rather than by spinning in step with the grid. A system with less rotating mass is a system with less time to react.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The two ideas interact rather than sitting side by side. The first is about matching energy over hours and is addressed by forecasting and storage; the second is about stability over seconds and is addressed by different equipment entirely, and a grid that solved only one of them would fail in a way the other could not predict.

title: Copyright and the Public Domain
standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Copyright is usually explained as a property right and is more accurately described as a bargain. The public grants an author exclusive rights for a period, in exchange for the work eventually belonging to everybody.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The exchange is stated plainly in the oldest statutes, which are less coy about it than modern discussion tends to be. An author receives a limited monopoly because that is expected to produce more works than would otherwise exist, and the limit on it is what the public receives in return for granting it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Both halves have moved since. Terms have been extended repeatedly in many jurisdictions, from an original period measured in a small number of years to one now commonly running for the author's life plus seventy years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The argument for extension is about incentive, and it is not a foolish argument. A longer term increases the expected return from creating a work, which should in principle mean that more works are created than would otherwise have been, and the argument has been put to legislatures many times and accepted by them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The counter-argument is about where the incentive can act. A term extension applies to works already written, and no incentive can operate backwards, so the part of an extension that covers existing works transfers value without producing anything.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The second idea concerns what the public domain is for, and it is not only about cost. Works out of copyright can be adapted, translated, annotated, digitised and reissued by anybody, and that produces activity which permission-based arrangements do not.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The hard case is the orphan work. A book whose rights holder cannot be identified or found is protected and unusable, so a library that digitises it risks a claim and the absence of a claimant is not a defence, and the work is effectively lost while remaining legally owned.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The two ideas build into a single analysis. Copyright is an exchange, and a term long enough that most works become orphaned before expiry is an exchange where one side delivers and the other delivers something nobody can collect.

title: The Rate at Which Soil Is Made
standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Soil is not dirt and it is not simply ground-up rock. It is a structured material containing mineral particles, decayed organic matter, living organisms, water and air, arranged in layers that take a very long time to form.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Formation is slow because it depends on weathering, which is slow. Rock is broken down physically and chemically, organic matter accumulates from whatever grows in it, and organisms mix the two, and all of that is measured in centimetres per century rather than per year.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Loss can be very fast, and the two rates are not of the same order. Soil moves when water or wind detaches particles and carries them away, and the rate at which that happens depends almost entirely on whether roots, residue or anything else is holding the surface in place when the rain arrives.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The asymmetry between those rates is the first idea and it is simple arithmetic. Where erosion under cultivation exceeds formation, the stock is being drawn down, and the fact that the drawdown is gradual makes it harder to notice rather than less real.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second idea concerns what makes soil productive, which is not the same as how much of it there is. Structure matters as much as depth: the aggregates that give soil its crumb, the pores that hold water, and the fungal networks that move nutrients.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those can be degraded without any soil leaving the field at all. Compaction from heavy machinery, loss of organic matter from continuous cultivation and disruption of fungal networks all reduce what a given depth of soil can do.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So there are two distinct problems that look like one from a distance. One is a quantity being physically removed, and the other is a quality being lost in place, and a measure that records only depth will miss the second entirely.

paras.label: H
paras.text: They also interact in a specific way, which is what makes the analysis complex rather than merely double. Degraded soil holds less water and binds less strongly, so it erodes faster, and the second problem accelerates the first while remaining invisible to anyone measuring only the first.

title: How Insulin Became a Medicine
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before 1922 a diagnosis of what is now called type 1 diabetes was fatal within months. The only treatment was a starvation diet, which postponed death by a short period at a cost that is difficult to read about, and physicians who used it understood exactly what they were doing.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The underlying idea had been available for decades. Experiments in the 1880s had shown that removing a dog's pancreas produced the disease, and it was understood that the organ secreted something whose absence was the cause, so the task was isolation rather than discovery.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The obstacle was chemical rather than conceptual, and it had defeated several capable researchers. The pancreas also produces digestive enzymes, which destroy the substance being sought during any ordinary attempt to extract it, so every preparation arrived inactive.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Frederick Banting, a surgeon with no research training, proposed tying off the ducts of the pancreas so that the enzyme-producing tissue would degenerate first. He took the idea to John Macleod at Toronto, who was unconvinced and supplied a laboratory, dogs and a student assistant, Charles Best, for the summer.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The first extracts worked in dogs and were far too impure for people. James Collip, a biochemist brought in afterwards, developed a purification method that made clinical use possible, and the first patient treated with the improved preparation recovered within days.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The credit was disputed immediately and the dispute was bitter. Banting and Macleod received the Nobel Prize in 1923, Banting announced he would share his half with Best, Macleod shared his with Collip, and the arrangement settled nothing about who had done what.

paras.label: G
paras.text: What happened next was unusual and is the part most often omitted. The patent was assigned to the University of Toronto for a nominal sum, on the stated reasoning that nobody should profit from a discovery of this kind, and licences were granted to manufacturers.

paras.text: The sequence is therefore a chain in which no element is sufficient. An old physiological idea, a procedural suggestion from an outsider, a laboratory he did not own, a purification he could not perform, and a decision about ownership that none of the science required.

title: The Making of the Marshall Plan
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the summer of 1947 the United States proposed to finance the reconstruction of European economies on a scale with no precedent. The programme is usually described as generous, and generosity is the least useful word available for understanding why it happened or what shape it took.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The situation it responded to was specific and had several components at once. European industrial production had not recovered, the winter of 1946 to 1947 had been severe, and countries needed dollars to buy American goods while having nothing the United States wanted to buy in exchange.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That last element is the one most often left out and it drives much of the rest. A trading partner who cannot pay is not only a humanitarian problem but a market that has disappeared, and American exporters were facing precisely that.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The political argument ran alongside the economic one and was stated openly in internal documents. Economic distress was understood as making communist parties stronger in western Europe, and reconstruction was accordingly a security measure as much as an economic one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The proposal's design reflected a judgement about how to make it acceptable. The offer was extended to all European states including the Soviet Union, on terms requiring participants to open their accounts and coordinate with each other, which the Soviet Union declined and required its neighbours to decline.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Some historians argue that the conditions were framed in the expectation of refusal, which would make the universal offer a political act rather than an invitation. Others argue the offer was genuine and the conditions followed from the need to justify the spending domestically.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The recipients were also required to cooperate with each other, which produced institutions nobody had planned. Committees established to allocate funds became permanent bodies, and the habit of coordinated economic decision-making in western Europe begins substantially here.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the plan's effects separate into kinds. The transfers themselves were large and were not the largest thing; what mattered more over time was the removal of a dollar shortage, and the creation of machinery for cooperation that outlasted the money by decades.

paras.text: The situation it answered was specific and had several components at once. European industrial production had not recovered, the winter of 1946 to 1947 had been severe, and countries needed dollars to buy American goods while having nothing the United States wanted to buy in exchange.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That last element is most often left out and it drives much of the rest. A trading partner who cannot pay is not only a humanitarian problem but a market that has disappeared, and American exporters were facing exactly that.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The political argument ran alongside the economic one and was stated openly in internal documents. Economic distress was understood as strengthening communist parties in western Europe. Reconstruction was a security measure as much as an economic one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The design reflected a judgement about how to make it acceptable. The offer went to all European states including the Soviet Union, on terms requiring participants to open their accounts and coordinate with each other. The Soviet Union declined and required its neighbours to decline.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Some historians argue the conditions were framed expecting refusal, which would make the universal offer a political act rather than an invitation. Others argue the offer was genuine and the conditions followed from the need to justify the spending at home.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Recipients were also required to cooperate with each other, which produced institutions nobody had planned. Committees set up to allocate funds became permanent bodies, and the habit of coordinated economic decision-making in western Europe begins substantially here.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the effects separate into kinds. The transfers were large and were not the largest thing. What mattered more over time was removing a dollar shortage, and creating machinery for cooperation that outlasted the money by decades.

questions.a: A trading partner who cannot pay is not only a humanitarian problem but a market that has disappeared, and American exporters were facing precisely that.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the dispute over whether refusal was expected) and paragraph H (i.e. what mattered more than the transfers).
Summarize why the Marshall Plan took the shape it did.

The offer went to all European states on conditions the Soviet Union rejected, historians dispute whether refusal was expected, and the requirement to cooperate created institutions that outlasted the money.

questions.q:
dollar shortage: a condition in which countries lack the currency needed to buy from a particular trading partner.
allocate: to divide funds between recipients, which the committees were created to do.
Describe the connection between the cooperation requirement and the institutions that followed.
questions.a: Recipients were required to cooperate with each other, so committees established to allocate funds became permanent bodies and coordinated economic decision-making in western Europe begins substantially there.

note: Paragraph F reports a live historical dispute without resolving it, which is the restraint this standard needs. Ask what evidence would settle it.

title: How Smallpox Was Eradicated
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Smallpox is the only human disease that has been deliberately eliminated from the world. The last naturally occurring case was in 1977, and the achievement is frequently described as a triumph of vaccination, which is accurate and leaves out the part that was difficult.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The disease had several features that made elimination conceivable at all, and they are not shared by most infections. It has no animal reservoir, so there is nowhere for it to persist outside people; it produces a visible rash, so cases can be identified without a laboratory; and survivors are immune for life.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The initial strategy was mass vaccination, aiming for a high proportion of each population. It worked in some places and stalled in others, because reaching eighty per cent of a population is achievable and the remaining fraction includes exactly the people hardest to reach.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The change in approach came from observation in the field. Teams in eastern Nigeria facing a vaccine shortage concentrated on finding cases and vaccinating everyone around each one, and transmission stopped at coverage levels far below what the models had said was required.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The reasoning behind that result is specific. Smallpox spreads through close contact rather than casually, so a chain of transmission can be broken by immunising a ring around each case, and the disease does not need to be removed from a population so much as cut off from its next host.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Implementing it required a surveillance system rather than a vaccination campaign. Rewards were offered for reporting cases, teams investigated each report, and the operational problem became finding the last cases in places with no health infrastructure and active conflict.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The political element was essential and is usually omitted. The programme ran through the 1960s and 1970s with cooperation between the United States and the Soviet Union, who were supplying vaccine and expertise to the same effort while opposed in nearly everything else.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The eradication is therefore the product of four things interacting: a biological accident in the disease's properties, a strategy discovered in the field rather than designed, an administrative system built to find cases, and a political arrangement that no epidemiology could have produced.

title: How the Interstates Were Routed
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The American interstate highway system was authorised in 1956 and built over three decades. The decision to build it is usually explained in two or three sentences, and the decision about where to put it took much longer and had different people making it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The national argument was made in terms of defence and commerce. A network permitting rapid movement between cities was presented as a strategic asset, and the legislation that funded it carried defence in its name, which helped secure support from members who were unenthusiastic about federal spending.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The engineering preference was for routes around cities. Through traffic does not need to enter a downtown, and a bypass is cheaper to build because it avoids acquiring expensive land and demolishing occupied buildings.

paras.label: D
paras.text: City governments frequently argued the opposite, and their reasons were their own. A highway through a city was expected to bring traffic to businesses, and federal money that paid for urban roadway was money a municipality did not have to raise.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There was a third motivation operating in many cities, and it is documented rather than inferred. Urban renewal programmes of the same period sought to clear districts described as blighted, and a highway route could accomplish a clearance that would otherwise require separate funding and separate justification.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The combination determined where the roads went. Routes ran through neighbourhoods with low property values and limited political representation, which lowered acquisition costs, satisfied renewal objectives and met the least organised resistance, and those three criteria selected the same places.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The consequences were durable because the structures are. A raised road divides a neighbourhood for as long as it stands, and several American cities are now spending substantial sums to remove or bury highways their predecessors were paid to build.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the interaction is between actors with different aims producing a single outcome. Federal engineers, municipal governments and renewal agencies each had a reason, no single one of those reasons explains the routes, and the routes are what all three wanted at once.

title: How the Atom Was Taken Apart
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: At the beginning of the twentieth century the atom was understood as indivisible, which is what the word had meant since it was coined. Within forty years it had been shown to have internal parts, and the sequence by which that happened is a chain in which each result created the next problem.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first step removed the indivisibility, and it did so from an experiment that had been running in various forms for decades. J. J. Thomson showed in 1897 that cathode rays consisted of particles far lighter than any atom and carrying a negative charge, which meant that atoms contained something smaller than themselves and therefore had parts.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That produced an immediate structural question. Matter is electrically neutral, so a negative component implies a positive one, and Thomson's own proposal distributed the positive charge through the volume of the atom with the electrons embedded in it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The proposal was testable and was tested. In 1909 an experiment in Ernest Rutherford's laboratory fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil, expecting slight deflections, and found that a small fraction came back toward the source.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Rutherford's interpretation required abandoning the distributed model entirely. A particle can only be reversed by something small, massive and concentrated, so the positive charge had to occupy a minute fraction of the atom's volume with the rest effectively empty.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The nuclear model created a problem of its own that classical physics could not solve. An electron orbiting a nucleus should radiate energy continuously and spiral inward within a fraction of a second, so the atoms described by the model should not exist.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Niels Bohr's response in 1913 was to impose a rule rather than derive one. Electrons occupy only certain allowed orbits and radiate only when moving between them, which was unjustified by anything then known and predicted the observed spectrum of hydrogen precisely.

paras.label: H
paras.text: A final element arrived much later. The nucleus had a mass inconsistent with its charge, and James Chadwick identified the neutron in 1932, which completed a picture built over thirty-five years by successive failures of the picture before it.

title: When a Definition Had to Be Rewritten
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: For most of history death required no definition, because the signs were unmistakable and simultaneous. Breathing stopped, the heart stopped, and the body cooled, and no circumstance existed in which a reasonable person would disagree about which state somebody was in.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Mechanical ventilation separated those signs for the first time. A machine can move air into lungs indefinitely, and a heart supplied with oxygen will continue beating, so a body can be maintained in a condition that previous centuries had no occasion to describe.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The term that emerged was brain death, and the history of that term is the history of a definition being refined under pressure. A committee at Harvard Medical School published criteria in 1968 that described an irreversible loss of all brain function, including the brainstem.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The criteria were operational rather than philosophical, and that was deliberate. They listed tests: unresponsiveness, absence of reflexes, absence of spontaneous breathing when the ventilator is withdrawn, and the exclusion of conditions that can imitate those findings, such as hypothermia or sedation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The exclusions are where the definition does most of its work. A barbiturate overdose can produce every listed sign and is reversible, so the criteria require that such causes be ruled out before the findings mean anything, and that requirement is part of the term rather than a caution attached to it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The word irreversible carries the greatest weight and is the least directly observable. No test demonstrates that a function will never return, so the criteria establish it by a combination of a known cause, a period of observation, and confirmation that nothing reversible is present.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Different jurisdictions then refined the term differently, which is what makes it useful to study. Some require loss of all brain function and some accept brainstem death, and a person can satisfy one definition and not the other while in exactly the same physical condition.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So this is a term that was created, tested against hard cases, divided into variants and continually restated. Its meaning is not something a dictionary can supply, because the word is doing a job that the practice of medicine keeps asking it to do more precisely.

title: The Word Terrorism in Three Statutes
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Terrorism is a word that carries enormous weight in public argument and has no single legal meaning. Different statutes in different countries define it differently, and the differences are not drafting variation but decisions with consequences attached.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Most definitions contain three elements in some combination. There is an act, usually violence or serious damage; there is an intention, usually to intimidate a population or compel a government; and there is a motivation, frequently described as political, religious or ideological.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The third element is the most contested and is absent from some definitions entirely. Requiring a political or ideological motive means that an identical act of violence falls inside or outside the definition depending on what a prosecutor can establish about the perpetrator's beliefs.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That requirement produces results that look inconsistent from outside a courtroom. Two attacks with similar methods and similar casualties can be charged differently, and the difference frequently rests on evidence about motive rather than on anything about what was done.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The breadth of the act element varies as much. Some definitions extend beyond violence against people to serious interference with electronic systems or disruption of essential services, which can bring conduct into the term that nobody drafting the first definitions had in view.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What the classification changes is substantial and specific. It alters available charges, sentencing, investigative powers, periods of detention before charge and the admissibility of certain evidence, so the definition is doing procedural work as well as descriptive work.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is a further layer in international law, where the absence of agreement is itself the fact. Efforts to produce a comprehensive definition have repeatedly stalled, largely over whether acts committed in the course of armed conflict or against occupying forces are included.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the term is refined in opposite directions by different authorities at the same time. A reader encountering it has to ask which definition is operating, because the word in a newspaper, the word in a statute and the word in a treaty negotiation are doing three different jobs.

title: How a Paper Refines Its Own Term
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension

paras.label: A

title: The Word Liberty in One Speech
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A political speech that uses one abstract word repeatedly is doing something more specific than repeating it. The word accumulates meaning as the speech goes on, and by the final occurrence it can be carrying a claim that the first occurrence did not contain.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Take liberty as the example, because it has been used in this way by speakers who disagreed with each other entirely. Its first appearance in a speech is almost always uncontroversial, invoked as a value the audience already holds and nobody present would dispute.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second occurrence usually attaches the word to something particular. Liberty becomes liberty to do a specified thing, or freedom from a specified interference, and a listener who accepted the first use is being asked to carry that acceptance to a narrower claim.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A third occurrence frequently contrasts it with something. Liberty is set against security, or against equality, or against order, and the contrast implies that the two cannot both be maximised, which is a substantial proposition offered without argument.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The structure works because the word does not change its tone. Each occurrence sounds like the same word with the same warmth, and the shifts in what it refers to are carried by the sentences around it rather than by the term itself.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Lincoln identified this directly in 1864, observing that the North and the South both used the word and meant incompatible things by it: one meaning a person's control of themselves, the other meaning a person's control of other people.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That observation names the technique from inside it. A speaker can rely on an audience supplying a meaning, and two audiences hearing the same sentence can supply different ones and both believe they have agreed with the speaker.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So tracking a key term through a speech means asking at each occurrence what it is attached to. The word is the same, and the proposition it belongs to is different, and a listener who hears only the word has heard the part designed to be agreeable.

title: What Natural Selection Does Not Mean
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Natural selection is a term whose two words both mislead, and whose author knew it and said so. Selection implies a selector and nature implies an agent, and the process the term names has neither.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Darwin borrowed the word from animal breeding deliberately. A breeder selects which animals reproduce, the results are visible within a lifetime, and the analogy let him show readers a process they had seen working before asking them to accept one they had not.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The analogy carries a cost he was aware of. In breeding there is someone with an intention, and in nature there is nothing corresponding to that, so the term suggests exactly the thing the theory was proposed to replace.

paras.label: D
paras.text: He responded by refining the term inside his own text. Later editions added language insisting that selection be understood as a metaphorical expression, and he wrote that he meant only the preservation of variations that happen to be advantageous.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A second phrase caused more trouble than the first and was not originally his. Survival of the fittest was coined by Herbert Spencer, adopted by Darwin in later editions at a colleague's suggestion, and it is the phrase that has done most of the subsequent damage.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The difficulty is that fittest in ordinary usage means strongest or healthiest, and in the technical sense it means whatever leaves more descendants in a particular environment. An organism that is smaller, slower and less impressive can be fitter in the only sense the theory uses.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The circularity objection follows directly from that, and it is worth stating properly. If the fittest are defined as those that survive, then survival of the fittest says only that those who survive survive, which is true and empty.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The answer is that fitness is not defined by survival but by traits that can be specified in advance. A biologist can predict which beak depth will do better in a drought and then measure whether it did, and that prediction is what converts a tautology into a claim.

title: When a Numbered List Is the Wrong Shape
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A numbered list is the most common structure in technical and official writing, and it carries an assumption that is frequently false. A list asserts that its items are of the same kind, independent of one another, and complete, and a great deal of material satisfies none of those conditions.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The independence assumption fails first and fails quietly. A list of five risks in which the third causes the fourth has presented a chain as a set, and a reader allocating attention evenly across five items has misallocated it, because addressing one of them would remove two.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The equality assumption fails next. Items in a list appear equivalent because they are formatted equivalently, so a list combining one catastrophic possibility with four inconveniences has flattened a difference that the document exists to communicate.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Completeness is implied by the form even where it is disclaimed. A list of seven causes reads as the causes, and a phrase such as among others placed before it does very little, because the shape of the page asserts more strongly than the sentence denies.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Prose handles all three cases better and is harder to scan, which is the genuine trade. A paragraph can say that the third factor produces the fourth, that one of them matters far more, and that the enumeration is partial, and a reader must then read it rather than skim.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There are structures that keep the scannability and fix the assumptions. A diagram shows dependency directly, a table with a severity column restores the differences between items, and a list divided under headings signals that the groups are not comparable.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Evaluating a document therefore means asking what its structure asserted without saying. A reader can test a list by asking whether any item causes another, whether any dwarfs the rest, and whether anything obvious is missing from it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Where the answer to all three is no, the list is the right shape and its clarity is a genuine achievement. Where the answer to any is yes, the document has made a claim through its formatting that it would not have been willing to make in a sentence.

title: The Report Organised by Theme
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: An inquiry into something that went wrong has to choose between two structures, and the choice is made early and shapes everything the report can show. It can proceed chronologically, or it can proceed by theme.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A chronological report follows the events in order, which is the arrangement most readers expect and the one most inquiries adopt by default. It is easy to follow, it establishes what was known to whom at each point in the sequence, and it makes a reader experience events in roughly the way the participants did.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That structure has a specific weakness. A cause that operated continuously throughout, such as a reporting line that discouraged bad news, appears nowhere in particular because it was everywhere, and a reader following the timeline meets it as a series of unconnected moments.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A thematic report inverts both properties at once. Organised under headings such as training, communication and oversight, it can state a persistent failure a single time and then support it properly with instances drawn from across the whole period under examination.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Its weakness is equally specific. The reader loses the sequence, and with it the ability to judge what any individual could reasonably have known at the time, which is precisely the question that matters when conduct rather than systems is being assessed.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Many inquiries attempt both and the attempt is usually visible in the structure. A narrative section establishes the sequence, thematic chapters follow, and the length doubles while the reader is required to hold the chronology in mind through the analysis.

paras.label: G
paras.text: What makes the choice evaluable rather than a matter of taste is the question the inquiry was set. An inquiry asked whether a system failed is well served by themes; an inquiry asked whether a person should have acted differently is not.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So a reader can assess a report's structure directly against its own terms of reference. Where the two match, the organisation does work for the reader, and where they do not, the report is answering its question in a shape that obscures the answer.

title: The Textbook That Starts With the Answer
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Textbook chapters are written in two opposite shapes, and the difference is not stylistic. One begins with the conclusion and explains it; the other reconstructs the problem and arrives at the conclusion at the end.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is the standard modern form, and its advantages are real rather than merely conventional. A chapter that states the principle in its opening paragraph gives a reader a framework to hang everything else on, and all the subsequent material is easier to follow because its destination is already known.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It also reflects how the field itself now thinks, which is not a trivial consideration. Presenting a settled result first is honest about the present state of knowledge, and a student is not asked to spend a week inside a confusion that the discipline resolved two centuries ago and has not revisited.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What it removes is the reason the result is believed. A principle stated first arrives with the authority of the textbook, and the evidence that follows reads as illustration of something already accepted rather than as the argument that established it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The reconstructive shape makes the opposite trade. A chapter that begins with the observations that puzzled people, and lets the reader feel the difficulty, produces understanding of why the answer is the answer, and does so slowly and at the cost of frustration.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is evidence that the slower form produces better retention and transfer, and evidence that it produces worse examination performance in the short term, and both findings can be true because they measure different things.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The decisive consideration is usually what comes next. A chapter that is a prerequisite for ten more is better written in the efficient form, and a chapter intended to show what the subject is actually like has a different job.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So a structure can be evaluated against a stated purpose rather than in the abstract. The question is not which shape is better but what the chapter is for, and a textbook that uses the same shape for everything has not asked.

title: Chronological or Thematic in a History
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A history of a long period has to be arranged, and the two available arrangements are incompatible in a way that cannot be resolved by careful writing. A book proceeds by time or by subject, and whichever it chooses, it loses what the other would have shown.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A chronological history preserves contingency, which is its great strength. A reader moving forward in time meets events in the order the participants did, without knowing what will happen, and the sense that things could have gone otherwise survives.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What it cannot show is a slow change. A shift in landholding or in family size happens across a century and appears in a chronological account as a series of small mentions, none of which conveys the magnitude of the whole.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A thematic history can state that change directly and support it properly. A chapter on landholding can compare the beginning and the end of the period, present the evidence together, and give the reader a quantity rather than an impression.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Its cost is that everything happens at once. A reader finishing a thematic chapter on agriculture and beginning one on religion returns to the start of the period, and the connections between the two domains, which operated in time, are hard to see.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those connections are frequently the point of the book. A change in landholding that caused a change in religious practice is a claim about sequence, and a structure that separates the two domains into different chapters makes that claim harder to state than to assert.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Some historians solve this by nesting. Large chronological sections contain thematic chapters, so the sequence is preserved at one scale and the themes are developed at another, which works where the period divides naturally and not otherwise.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Evaluating the structure therefore means asking what the book claims. A book arguing that one development caused another needs the sequence visible, and a book arguing that a society had a particular character does not, and a structure that fights the argument is a real defect rather than a preference.

title: The Argument Built on a Diagram
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Some expositions are built around a single diagram, and the prose exists to explain it. That is a structural choice as substantial as any ordering of paragraphs, and it has consequences the writer may not have intended.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its first effect is that the argument becomes available at a glance. A reader who understands the figure has the claim, and the text that follows is confirmation rather than construction, which is why such pieces are easy to remember.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its second effect is that the diagram's limitations become the argument's limitations. A figure showing two axes can represent two variables, so a third one has to appear in the prose, and material that appears only in the prose of a diagram-led piece is routinely forgotten.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third effect concerns what a diagram asserts by its form. Boxes joined by arrows assert that the relationships are directional and discrete, and a process that is continuous or that runs in both directions has been misrepresented by the shape before any label is read.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A well-made piece turns these into strengths deliberately. The figure carries the claims that are genuinely discrete and directional, the prose carries what cannot be drawn, and the text says explicitly that the diagram simplifies in a stated way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A badly made one lets the figure do work it cannot support. An arrow drawn between two boxes looks like a demonstrated relationship whether the evidence for it is strong or absent, and a reader cannot tell which arrows are which.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Evaluating such a structure means reading the figure and the text against each other. Every arrow should correspond to a claim defended somewhere in the prose, and every claim that matters should be visible in the figure or explicitly marked as not drawn.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Where that correspondence holds, the structure is extremely effective and deserves the reputation it has. Where it does not, the piece has acquired the persuasive force of a diagram without the evidence a diagram implies, and the mismatch is invisible to a reader looking only at the picture.

title: The Shortest Important Paper
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In April 1953 Nature published a paper about the structure of DNA that runs to roughly a page. It is among the most consequential scientific papers of the century, and much of its effect comes from decisions about style that could have been made differently.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The opening sentence does something unusual for a technical paper. It announces a structure and calls it of considerable biological interest, which is a claim about significance offered before any evidence and in a register closer to understatement than to announcement.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second paragraph disposes of a rival. It describes an earlier proposed structure, states precisely why it cannot be right, and moves on, which takes four sentences and removes the main competing account from the reader's mind before the new one is presented.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The description itself is almost entirely geometric. Two chains, coiled around a common axis, running in opposite directions, with the bases on the inside and the backbones outside, and the whole arrangement is conveyed without a single equation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The pairing rule arrives as a constraint rather than a discovery. The text observes that only specific pairs of bases can fit the available space, which presents a chemical fact as a consequence of the geometry rather than as an additional assumption.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Then comes the sentence the paper is remembered for. It observes that the specific pairing immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material, and declines to say more, and the restraint is the effect.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The restraint was also strategic, which the authors did not conceal in later accounts. Stating the implication fully would have required evidence they did not have, and stating it this way claimed the territory without making a claim that could be refuted.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the power of the piece comes from compression and from what it refuses to do. It has no speculation, no survey of the field and no discussion section, and a reader finishes it in three minutes having been shown a structure and handed its most important consequence in one clause.

title: The Last Sentence of a Book
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The closing sentence of On the Origin of Species is one of the most quoted in English scientific writing, and its effect is produced by techniques that can be described precisely, which is what makes it worth studying rather than merely admiring.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The passage begins by asking the reader to look at a tangled bank, with plants, birds, insects and worms, and the choice of scene is doing work. It is ordinary, it is local, and it is the kind of place a reader has stood in without thinking about it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The sentence then lists the laws that produced everything on the bank, and the list is long. Growth, reproduction, inheritance, variability, a struggle for life, and the consequences that follow from them, delivered in a sequence that accumulates rather than resolves.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The accumulation is the technique. Each clause adds a law, the sentence refuses to end, and the reader's sense of how much is being accounted for grows with the syntax rather than being stated by it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The final movement reverses the scale without changing the subject. From a bank in a field, the sentence moves to the planet cycling according to a fixed law, and places the whole of the preceding list inside that motion.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The last clause has been the subject of attention for a century and a half. Endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved: three adjectives, a tense that includes the present, and a passive construction that names no agent.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That absence of an agent is the argument of the book compressed into a grammatical choice. A sentence written actively would require a subject doing the evolving, and the passive leaves the forms arriving from the laws listed earlier and from nothing else.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the beauty and the content are not separable here, which is the strongest version of what this standard asks. The passage is moving because of its structure, and its structure is a statement of the theory, and a paraphrase loses the argument along with the cadence.

title: The Letter That Is Not Angry
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A letter written in reply to a public and unjust accusation has two available registers, and the choice between them is made in the first sentence. It determines almost everything about what the letter can subsequently accomplish, and it cannot be revised halfway through without the revision itself becoming the subject.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is anger, and it has real advantages. It conveys the scale of the wrong, it is honest about what the writer feels, and it will satisfy readers who already agree, which is a larger group than writers usually estimate.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its disadvantage is specific rather than moral. An angry letter allows a reader who wishes to avoid the substance to discuss the tone instead, and the discussion of tone can proceed indefinitely without anyone addressing the accusation.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second register is controlled, and its power depends entirely on the reader understanding that it is controlled rather than merely mild. A letter that is measured about something outrageous produces a gap between the matter and the manner, and the reader fills that gap themselves, which is the whole of the effect.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The technique that makes this work is usually understatement. A writer who describes a serious wrong in plain and unemphatic language invites the reader to supply the emphasis, and an emphasis a reader supplies is held more firmly than one they were given.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A second technique is the conceded point. Granting something to the accuser, early and without qualification, establishes that the writer is capable of concession, which makes every subsequent refusal to concede weigh more than it otherwise would.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The third is the question that cannot be answered comfortably. A direct question, asked politely, leaves a reader composing an answer in their own head, and a reader who cannot produce one has been persuaded by their own silence.

paras.label: H
paras.text: None of this is a recommendation of calm over anger as a general matter. It is an observation about what each register makes possible, and the controlled letter is harder to write, harder to sustain and considerably harder to dismiss.
