title: The Understatement in a Report
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Official reports into serious failures are written in a register that strikes many first-time readers as inadequate to the subject. The language is flat, the verbs are weak, and the findings arrive in sentences that seem to be working hard not to be interesting.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some of that flatness is defensive, and the legal pressures producing it have been discussed elsewhere. What is less often noticed is that the restraint, in a well-written report, is also a deliberate rhetorical instrument, and that it is frequently the most effective one available to the people writing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The mechanism is contrast. A sentence recording that a request for additional staffing was submitted on four occasions and not acknowledged is doing nothing dramatic, and the drama is supplied entirely by the reader placing it beside the outcome.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Juxtaposition without comment does similar work. A paragraph that gives the date of a warning and then, in the next sentence, the date of the failure has made an argument without a single evaluative word appearing anywhere in it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The technique depends absolutely on the surrounding register being consistent. A report that is flat throughout makes each factual sentence land, and a report that permits itself one indignant paragraph has taught the reader that the flatness was a choice and can be departed from.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is a further effect that is specific to this genre. A reader who has supplied the outrage themselves will defend the conclusion more firmly than one who was handed it, because they have done the work and will not lightly treat it as having been done for them.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The register also has a cost, and the better reports know it. Families and those directly affected frequently find the flatness unbearable, and a document that is maximally persuasive to a minister can be experienced as an institution refusing to say plainly what happened.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Some reports address this directly by changing register once, in a preface, where a chairman writes in the first person. That single departure works precisely because the rest does not, which is the whole technique stated in a paragraph.

paras.text: Some reports address this by changing register once, in a preface, where a chairman writes in the first person. That single departure works precisely because the rest does not, which is the whole technique stated in a paragraph.

questions.a: A paragraph giving the date of a warning and then the date of the failure makes an argument without a single evaluative word appearing in it.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. the cost of the register) and paragraph H (i.e. the single departure in a preface).
Summarize how restraint works in an official report.
questions.a: Flat language lets a factual sentence land beside an outcome the reader supplies the force for, and juxtaposed dates argue without evaluative words. The effect requires the register to be consistent, a reader who supplies the outrage defends the conclusion more firmly, and the cost is that those directly affected may experience the flatness as a refusal to say what happened.

evaluative: expressing a judgement, which the register deliberately avoids.

questions.a: A report that permits itself one indignant paragraph has taught the reader that the flatness was a choice and can be departed from, which weakens the effect elsewhere.

note: Paragraph G is the one that keeps this honest. The most persuasive document and the most humane one are not always the same document.

title: The Speech Built on One Repetition
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Anaphora is the repetition of the same words at the beginning of successive clauses, and it is the oldest device in persuasive speech. It survives because it does several things at once that are difficult to achieve separately.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its first function is structural, and it is felt by an audience rather than consciously noticed by them. A repeated opening tells a listener where each new unit begins, which matters enormously in speech, where a listener cannot see a paragraph break, cannot go back, and has only the sound to navigate by.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second function is accumulation. Each repetition adds an instance to a set the listener is assembling, and the force comes from the number rather than from any individual item, which is why removing three examples from such a passage weakens it more than removing three ordinary sentences.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is anticipation. After the third repetition a listener knows the form of the fourth, and the brief moment of knowing what is coming produces a kind of participation that passive listening does not.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That anticipation is also what makes the ending dangerous and powerful. A speaker who breaks the pattern deliberately at the last item produces a sharp effect, and one who breaks it accidentally produces an anticlimax the audience will feel without being able to name.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The device is not neutral between arguments, which is worth stating plainly. It works best for claims that are genuinely multiple, where many instances exist, and it can create an impression of multiplicity where a speaker has two real examples and three weak ones.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A listener can test this directly and in real time. Take the repeated passage, remove the repetition, and read the items as a plain list, and a set of strong instances survives that treatment while a padded one visibly collapses.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the device is powerful because it is doing legitimate work and is available for illegitimate work with the same syntax. The form tells a listener that there are many reasons, and whether there are is a separate question the form does not address.

title: Deciding Whether a Bridge Is Safe
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A local authority has to decide whether a bridge can remain open. The question is concrete, the answer has to be given by a date, and the information available to answer it arrives in four forms that do not resemble each other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is the original design. Drawings and calculations from the period of construction state what the structure was built to carry, and they are the only document that says what the designer intended, which is not the same as what was built.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is the inspection record, which is not a measurement at all but a sequence of judgements made by people. Inspectors record visible condition against defined categories, and a series of such records shows a trajectory over time, which is frequently far more informative than any single assessment taken on its own.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is instrumental. Strain gauges, crack monitors and displacement sensors produce continuous numerical data, and they measure precisely what they are placed to measure and nothing at all about anywhere they are not.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth is a model. A structural analysis predicts how loads distribute through the bridge, and its output is as good as its assumptions about material condition, which are supplied by the inspections and the measurements rather than by the model.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Integrating these is not a matter of averaging. They disagree in a structured way: the design says what should be there, the inspection says what can be seen, the instruments say what one point is doing, and the model says what follows if the first three are right.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The decisive questions are usually about the gaps between them. A model predicting stress at a location nobody can inspect, and nobody has instrumented, is producing a number with nothing behind it, and knowing that is worth more than the number.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the engineer's judgement is about which source governs where. Visible deterioration overrides a model, an instrument reading that contradicts an inspection prompts a second inspection rather than a conclusion, and the design drawing is evidence about intention and never about present condition.

title: Deciding Where to Put a School
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A district has to site a new school, and the decision is irreversible for sixty years. The inputs arrive from different places, in different formats, with different reliabilities, and none of them answers the question on its own.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Demographic projections come first and are the least certain thing in the process. A forecast of how many five-year-olds will live in an area in eight years depends on birth rates, on migration and on housing that has not been built.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Housing plans are a separate source and they interact with the first. Approved developments supply a number of dwellings with a timescale, and converting dwellings into children requires an assumption about household composition that varies with the kind of housing built.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Travel data answers a different question again. Catchment modelling shows how far children would travel to each candidate site and by what mode, and a site that is central on a map can be badly placed once a river, a main road or a railway is taken into account.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Cost information constrains everything and is the most precise and least flexible input. Land acquisition, ground conditions and construction costs are quantified to a degree the other sources cannot match, which gives them an influence their importance may not justify.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Consultation supplies something none of the others can. Residents know which crossings are dangerous, which routes are walked and which are not, and a site that models well can be opposed for reasons the models had no way to contain.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Integrating these means noticing that they have different time horizons. Cost is a figure for next year, travel patterns change over a decade, and demography is a projection about a generation, and a decision that optimises the precise short-term input will be judged against the uncertain long-term one.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The usual failure is therefore predictable rather than exotic. The most quantified source dominates because it is the easiest to defend in a document, and the least quantified one turns out to have been describing the thing that mattered.

title: Deciding Whether to Evacuate
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: An official has to decide whether to order an evacuation ahead of a storm, and the decision has to be made before the information that would settle it exists. Everything available at the moment of decision is a projection, and the costs of being wrong are asymmetric and both large.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The forecast is the first input and it is a distribution rather than a path. Models produce a range of possible tracks, the commonly published cone represents where the centre is likely to go, and a reader who treats the cone's edge as the edge of the danger has misread it entirely.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Physical exposure data is a separate layer. Elevation models, flood mapping and storm surge projections state which areas go under at which water heights, and these are static, well-understood and among the most reliable things in the whole picture.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Population data answers who is there, and it is reliable in a way that is also misleading. A census records residence, and the number of people in a coastal area on a given weekend can differ from the resident population by a very large factor.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Transport capacity determines whether the decision is executable at all. Road capacity, fuel availability and the time required to move a given population out are calculable, and they set a deadline that is independent of the storm and earlier than the storm.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Vulnerability information is the least quantified and the most consequential. Which residents cannot drive, which require medical equipment and which will not leave are questions that determine whether an order produces an evacuation or produces a traffic jam containing the people most at risk.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The integration problem is that these have incompatible update rates. The forecast changes every six hours, the transport deadline is fixed, and the vulnerability information is months old, so the decision has to be made on the schedule set by the slowest component.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is why an evacuation decision is made earlier than the evidence justifies, and why that is correct rather than cautious. Waiting for a better forecast means passing the point at which the roads can still clear, and the choice is between acting on a distribution and losing the ability to act.

title: Deciding What a Painting Is
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A painting is offered for sale as the work of a particular artist, and the question of whether it is cannot be answered by looking, although looking is where it starts and sometimes where it ends.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Connoisseurship is the oldest source and much the hardest to evaluate from outside the discipline. A specialist who has examined hundreds of works by an artist recognises handling in a way they frequently cannot articulate, and such judgements have been right often enough to matter and wrong often enough that they cannot be allowed to stand alone.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Provenance is documentary rather than physical. An unbroken chain of ownership running back to the artist's own studio is the strongest single piece of evidence available, and its weakness is that documents can be fabricated and that gaps in a chain are extremely common for entirely innocent reasons.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Technical analysis supplies constraints rather than attributions. X-ray and infrared imaging reveal underdrawing and changes beneath the surface, and those reveal how a picture was built, which is a different question from who built it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Material analysis answers questions with dates attached. A pigment that was not manufactured until 1830 cannot be in a painting from 1780, and that is a decisive negative result which no amount of connoisseurship can overturn.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The asymmetry there is the key to the whole exercise. Material evidence can refute an attribution absolutely and can never confirm one, because a skilled forger using period materials leaves nothing for the analysis to find.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the sources are not of equal kind and cannot be weighed on one scale. One can disprove, one can establish a chain, one describes method, and one is expert judgement, and a case is built by seeing whether any of them produces a refutation.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What follows is a specific and unsatisfying conclusion that the field accepts. An attribution is a best current judgement rather than a determination, and a painting can move between categories as evidence accumulates, which is why catalogues record the reasoning as well as the conclusion.

title: Deciding Whether to Approve a Drug
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A regulator has to decide whether a medicine may be sold. The decision is binary, the evidence is not, and the material presented arrives in formats that have to be assessed against each other rather than added together.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Trial results are the centre of the submission and are by a long way the most structured input the regulator receives. They state effects in defined populations with stated statistical properties, and their principal limitation lies in who was studied rather than in how carefully the study was conducted.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Trial populations are routinely narrower than the population that will receive the drug. Participants are often younger, with fewer other conditions and fewer other medications, so the evidence is strongest about people least like the average eventual patient.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Safety data arrives from a different direction and in a quite different shape from efficacy data. Adverse events are counted as rates across the whole programme, and a serious effect occurring in one patient in five thousand will frequently not appear even once in a trial programme that enrolled three thousand people.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Manufacturing information is assessed separately and is not about the molecule. It establishes that what was tested can be produced consistently, and a product that cannot be made to specification reliably is not approvable however well it performed.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Patient testimony enters through formal channels and supplies something the trials do not measure. It describes what a condition is like and which outcomes matter to people living with it, which is frequently not what the trial chose as its endpoint.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The integration problem is that these answer different questions and none is decisive. Efficacy, safety, manufacturability and relevance are separate assessments, and a submission can be strong in three and fail on the fourth.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What the decision ultimately rests on is a comparison against the alternative rather than against perfection. A drug for a condition with no existing treatment is assessed on terms that a fourth drug for a well-treated condition is not, and the same evidence can support approval in one case and refusal in the other.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A regulator has to decide whether a medicine may be sold. The decision is binary, the evidence is not, and the material arrives in formats that have to be assessed against each other rather than added together.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Trial results are the centre of the submission and the most structured input. They state effects in defined populations with stated statistical properties. Their main limitation is in who was studied rather than in how carefully.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Trial populations are routinely narrower than the population that will receive the drug. Participants are often younger, with fewer other conditions and fewer other medications. The evidence is strongest about people least like the average eventual patient.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Safety data arrives from a different direction and in a different shape. Adverse events are counted as rates. A serious effect occurring in one patient in five thousand will frequently not appear at all in a programme of three thousand people.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Manufacturing information is assessed separately and is not about the molecule. It establishes that what was tested can be produced consistently. A product that cannot be made to specification reliably is not approvable however well it performed.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Patient testimony enters through formal channels and supplies what trials do not measure. It describes what a condition is like and which outcomes matter to people living with it, which is frequently not what the trial chose as its endpoint.

paras.text: The integration problem is that these answer different questions and none is decisive. Efficacy, safety, manufacturability and relevance are separate assessments. A submission can be strong in three and fail on the fourth.

questions.a: An effect occurring in one patient in five thousand will frequently not appear at all in a trial programme of three thousand people.

adverse event: a harmful occurrence recorded during a trial, counted as a rate.

questions.a: A drug for a condition with no existing treatment is assessed on terms a fourth drug for a well-treated condition is not, so the same evidence can support approval in one case and refusal in the other.

note: Pairs with grade 10's How a Drug Is Shown to Work. That article was about producing the evidence and this is about deciding on it.

title: Marbury and the Power to Decide
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1803 the Supreme Court of the United States decided a case about a commission that had not been delivered, and the decision established that the Court may declare an act of Congress unconstitutional. The reasoning by which it got there is more interesting than the holding.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The facts of the case were small and the politics surrounding it were not. A departing administration had made a series of appointments at the last possible moment, the incoming Secretary of State declined to deliver some of the resulting commissions, and William Marbury went to the Court and asked it to order delivery.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The Court faced a trap with no comfortable exit. Ordering delivery would produce an order the administration could simply ignore, demonstrating that the Court could be defied, and refusing would concede that the executive could withhold what the law required.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The opinion takes the questions in a deliberate order, and the order is the whole manoeuvre. It asks first whether Marbury has a right to the commission, and answers yes; second whether the law affords a remedy, and answers yes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Those two answers are a rebuke to the administration delivered before anything else happens, and they cost the Court nothing, because no order has yet been issued that anybody could refuse to obey.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The third question is whether this Court can supply that remedy, and here the opinion turns. The statute under which Marbury applied gave the Court power the Constitution had not given it, so the statute conflicted with the Constitution.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The conclusion follows from a premise stated as though it were obvious. A written constitution is superior law, a court deciding a case must apply the law, and where two laws conflict a court must say which governs, which is a chain any reader can follow and which nothing in the text explicitly authorises.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the Court declined jurisdiction and acquired a power. It gave the administration the outcome it wanted, refused Marbury his commission, and established in the course of doing so a principle that has been the foundation of its authority ever since.

title: The Dissent That Became the Law
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1896 the Supreme Court upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railway carriages for Black and white passengers. The decision was seven to one, and the single dissent is now better known than the majority opinion it failed to prevent.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The majority's reasoning proceeded from a distinction it treated as straightforward. A law requiring separation, it held, does not of itself impose inequality, so a requirement applying to both races equally is not a discrimination that the Fourteenth Amendment reaches.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then addressed the obvious objection with an argument about perception. If separation is felt as a badge of inferiority, the opinion stated, that is because the group affected chooses to construe it so, which locates the harm in the reaction rather than in the law.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Justice John Marshall Harlan's dissent attacks both steps and attacks the second first. He states that everyone knows what the statute is for, that nobody is deceived about which carriage is which, and that the Court's reasoning depends on a pretence it does not believe.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The dissent's central passage is a claim about what a constitution does rather than about railways. It argues that the document neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens, and that this is the principle the majority has set aside while claiming to apply it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: He then makes a prediction, which is the most quoted element and the part a reader should examine most carefully. He writes that the judgement will in time prove as pernicious as an earlier decision the Court had by then repudiated entirely.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The dissent is not an unqualified document and is weaker in places that are usually omitted. The same opinion contains a passage asserting the enduring dominance of one race, which sits uneasily beside the sentence it is best known for.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Nearly sixty years later a unanimous Court reached the conclusion the dissent had argued for, which is why this is the standard case for the proposition that a losing argument can be the correct one and can be preserved by being written down.

title: The Concurrence That Became the Framework
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1952, during a labour dispute that threatened steel production in wartime, the President ordered the seizure of the steel mills. The Supreme Court held the seizure unlawful, and the opinion that has governed the question since was not the opinion of the Court.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The majority opinion reasoned from the absence of authorisation. No statute permitted the seizure, Congress had considered and rejected such a power, and the Constitution does not grant the executive a general power to take property, so the action had no legal basis.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Justice Robert Jackson agreed with the outcome and wrote separately, beginning with an observation about the method rather than the case. He noted that arguments about executive power are usually conducted by quoting isolated clauses and historical materials selectively, and that this produces confident conclusions in both directions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: His alternative was to sort the question into three categories according to what Congress had done. That move is the entire contribution, and it converted a question about the extent of a power into a question about a relationship between two branches.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In the first category the President acts with express or implied authorisation from Congress, and the authority is at its maximum, because it combines what the office holds with what the legislature has granted.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In the second the President acts where Congress has neither granted nor denied, a zone Jackson called twilight, in which the outcome is likely to depend on practice and circumstance rather than on an abstract allocation.

paras.label: G
paras.text: In the third the President acts against the expressed or implied will of Congress, and the authority is at its lowest, because it rests on the office's own powers minus whatever the legislature may constitutionally exercise over the matter.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The seizure fell into the third category, which decided the case, and the framework has been applied far beyond it since. A concurrence joined by no other justice became the operative law because it supplied a structure rather than an answer, which is a specific and unusual kind of persuasive achievement.

title: Federalist Fifty-One
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Federalist 51 addresses a problem that the earlier papers in the series had raised repeatedly and had not solved. A government has to be strong enough to actually govern and limited enough not to become dangerous to the people it governs, and those two requirements pull directly against each other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The essay rejects the obvious remedy before it proposes its own, which is why the rejection comes first. Relying on the quality of the people who hold office is dismissed, not from cynicism about any particular individual, but because an arrangement that works only when the officials are good is not really an arrangement at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The famous formulation states the problem with unusual symmetry. If men were angels no government would be necessary, and if angels governed men no controls on government would be necessary, which locates the whole difficulty in the fact that neither condition holds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The proposed mechanism is structural and is stated plainly as a design principle. Ambition must be made to counteract ambition, so the interest of the person must be connected with the constitutional rights of the place.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That sentence does something specific that is easy to pass over. It does not ask officials to restrain themselves; it arranges for each branch to defend its own position out of self-interest, which converts a moral requirement into an institutional one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The essay then extends the argument to society rather than only to government. A multiplicity of interests makes oppressive combinations harder to assemble, which is the argument of Federalist 10 reappearing in a different application.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The reasoning is open to a direct objection that the essay does not fully answer. The design assumes that officeholders identify with their branch rather than with a party spanning several branches, and party loyalty can align the interests the structure assumed would conflict.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That objection is worth holding because it is testable against two centuries of practice. The question is whether a structure designed to set institutions against each other works when the people in them are organised into groups the design did not anticipate.

title: The Reasoning of Brown
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1954 the Supreme Court held unanimously that segregated public schools violate the Fourteenth Amendment. The opinion is short, it is deliberately plain, and the reasoning by which it reaches its conclusion is not the reasoning most people assume.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The Court begins by examining the history of the Amendment and declines to rest on it. The evidence about what its framers intended for public education is described as inconclusive, partly because public education in 1868 was so limited that the question had barely arisen.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That move is significant and is a choice rather than a necessity. Having found the historical argument indeterminate, the Court states that it cannot turn the clock back and must consider public education as it exists now, which is a decision about how a constitution should be read.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The opinion then establishes the importance of education in contemporary terms. It describes schooling as the foundation of citizenship and the principal instrument by which a child is prepared for life, and this paragraph is doing work that the historical section could not.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The central question is then narrowed with precision. The issue is not whether facilities are equal in buildings and salaries, because the Court assumes they are; the issue is whether separation itself deprives children of equal educational opportunity.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The answer rests on a claim about effect, and the opinion supports it with a citation that has been argued about ever since. A footnote lists psychological and social scientific studies, which is unusual in constitutional reasoning and was understood as unusual at the time.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Critics have objected that resting a constitutional holding on social science makes it vulnerable to the next study, and defenders reply that the studies were corroboration rather than foundation, and that the sentence they support states something the law already implied.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The opinion then does something procedurally distinctive. It declines to order a remedy, setting that question for later argument, which produced a second decision and a much slower implementation than the clarity of the first opinion suggested.

title: The Mayflower Compact
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning

paras.label: A
paras.text: In November 1620 a group aboard a ship off the coast of what is now Massachusetts signed a document of about two hundred words. title: Common Sense
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Thomas Paine's pamphlet appeared in January 1776 and sold in numbers that remain extraordinary relative to the population. Its argument had been made before in various forms, and the reason this version mattered is almost entirely a matter of how it was written.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The prose is the first thing to notice because it was the first thing contemporaries noticed. Paine writes in short declarative sentences, uses almost no Latin, cites scripture rather than classical authority, and addresses a reader who is assumed to be intelligent and not educated.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That choice had a political consequence beyond its literary one. A pamphlet written in this register could be read aloud in a tavern to people who could not read it themselves, which made the argument available to an audience that previous political writing had not addressed.

paras.label: D

By the time the pamphlet discusses the current king, it has already argued that hereditary succession is absurd in principle, so the specific grievances arrive as instances rather than as the case.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The argument against hereditary rule is made by reduction rather than by assertion. Paine observes that it requires believing that the merit of an original ruler, itself usually obtained by force, transmits through a bloodline indefinitely, and that nothing in observation supports this.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The economic argument is made in the same plain terms and is frequently underestimated. The pamphlet asserts that the connection to Britain damages American trade by involving the colonies in European wars they have no interest in, which is an argument addressed to merchants.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Paine then refuses the available compromise explicitly. Reconciliation, he argues, would leave the same arrangement in place and would simply postpone the question, which closes off the position most of his readers currently held.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The rhetorical achievement is therefore the removal of a middle. Before the pamphlet, a reader could want redress without wanting independence; after it, the pamphlet has argued that those are the same question, and that is the shift its enormous circulation carried.

title: The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom was drafted by Thomas Jefferson in 1777 and was not enacted until 1786, after a legislative fight that ran for most of a decade. Jefferson asked that it be named on his gravestone, alongside the Declaration and the founding of a university, and that his presidency should not be.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its structure is unusual for a statute and is the reason it reads as an argument. The operative provision is brief, and it is preceded by a long preamble that sets out the reasoning at a length no modern drafter would permit.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The preamble begins from a claim about the mind rather than about rights. It asserts that God created the mind free, and that attempts to influence it by punishment produce only hypocrisy, which is an argument about efficacy before it is one about justice.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It then makes a claim about what compulsion actually achieves. A person compelled to support an opinion they disbelieve is not persuaded, and the practice corrupts the religion it is meant to serve by filling it with people who do not hold it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third argument concerns the capacity of officials. The preamble observes that magistrates who judge opinions are fallible and will impose their own, and that the same power used well by one will be used badly by the next.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The operative sentence is then short and absolute. No person shall be compelled to attend or support any religious worship, nor suffer on account of religious opinion, nor shall their civil capacities be affected by it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The final paragraph does something rare in legislation and is worth reading closely. It acknowledges that a legislature cannot bind its successors, declares the rights asserted to be natural rights, and states that any future repeal would be an infringement of natural right.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is a statement about the status of the law rather than its content. The statute cannot prevent its own repeal and says so, and then characterises repeal in advance, which is a rhetorical device operating entirely outside the law's enforceable effect.

title: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Frederick Douglass delivered an address in Rochester, New York, on the fifth of July, 1852, having been invited by a local society to speak on the occasion of Independence Day. The date on which he chose to deliver it is the first element of the argument, and it was understood as such by everybody present.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The opening third of the speech praises the founders without qualification. It describes them as great men, calls their act brave, and affirms the principles of the Declaration in terms that any audience at such an event would expect and approve.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That section is not preliminary and it is not insincere. It establishes that the speaker accepts the standard the occasion invokes, which is the only position from which the rest of the speech can be delivered at all.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The turn is marked by a single pronoun and is among the most studied transitions in American oratory. Douglass moves from the achievements of your fathers to the question of what those achievements mean to him and to those he speaks for.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The question that follows is the title and it is constructed to be unanswerable in the terms of the occasion. He asks what the Fourth of July is to the American slave, and answers that it reveals to him the injustice and cruelty of which he is the constant victim.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What follows is not an accusation of falsehood but of inconsistency, and the distinction is the engine of the entire speech. The principles are not disputed; they are accepted, and the argument is that the nation does not apply them.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The method is therefore to use the audience's own document against their practice. A listener who had agreed with the opening third has already granted the premise from which the indictment follows, and cannot withdraw it without abandoning the occasion.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That makes this the clearest case in nineteenth-century American oratory of a foundational text being turned on the people who honour it. The speech does not ask for new principles, which is what makes it difficult to answer.

title: Civil Disobedience
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Henry David Thoreau's essay was published in 1849, following a night he spent in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax. The refusal was a protest against a war he opposed and against slavery, and the essay reasons outward from an act that was, in itself, extremely small.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its starting claim is about the relationship between a citizen and a law. Thoreau argues that a person's first obligation is to do what they believe right, and that obedience to law is owed only where law and right coincide.

paras.label: C
paras.text: He is explicit about the consequence for majority rule. A majority decides questions not because it is more likely to be right but because it is stronger, which he states plainly, and that observation is the premise from which the rest proceeds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The essay then distinguishes between kinds of complicity, which is where its argument becomes specific. A person who disapproves of an injustice while paying for it is participating in it, and the payment is the point at which an opinion becomes an action.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The remedy proposed is withdrawal rather than resistance. He does not advocate the overthrow of a government or violence against it; he argues for refusing to lend it practical support, which is a narrower position than the essay is often remembered as holding.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The willingness to accept punishment is essential and is frequently omitted from summaries. Thoreau's argument requires that the person refusing accept the legal consequence, because accepting it is what distinguishes the position from simple evasion.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The essay has a weakness its admirers acknowledge. It addresses a person who can afford to withdraw, and a man who can spend a night in jail and return to his life is differently placed from somebody whose dependents rely on their continued liberty.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Its later influence is nevertheless documented rather than asserted. Figures including Gandhi and King described reading it and taking from it the argument that an unjust law may be disobeyed openly by a person willing to accept the penalty, which is precisely the structure the essay set out.

title: The Man Who Lived Without a Clock
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1962 a French geologist named Michel Siffre spent two months in a cave beneath a glacier, deliberately and entirely without any means of telling the time. He had gone there to study the ice underground and ended up conducting, more or less by accident, a long experiment on himself.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The arrangement was deliberate and the conditions underground were severe. He had no watch, no daylight and no indication of the hour at any point, and a surface team logged the times at which he telephoned them while telling him nothing whatever about when those calls had occurred.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What he reported afterwards was a discrepancy. He believed he had been underground considerably less time than he had, and his own count of days had fallen behind the calendar by a substantial margin.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The explanation offered then was that an internal clock continues running without external cues and runs slightly slow. In the absence of light to reset it, a person's day drifts longer than twenty-four hours, and the accumulated difference is what Siffre had experienced.

paras.label: E
paras.text: He conducted considerably longer isolations afterwards, including six months in a Texas cave in 1972, and the later work recorded sleep and waking in far more detail, with better instrumentation, continuous monitoring and medical oversight throughout.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What those records showed was less tidy than the first account. Cycles were not uniformly long; some stretched to forty-eight hours, a few participants in related studies settled near twenty-five, and the pattern varied between individuals and over time.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Later research has substantially revised the interpretation while confirming the phenomenon. The free-running period is now understood to be close to twenty-four hours in most people, and several early estimates were affected by the lighting the participants themselves controlled.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode is therefore a useful case of how a finding matures. A striking first result turned out to be real in its central claim and wrong in its numbers, corrected by work that was possible only because the first result made the question seem worth asking.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. what the later records showed) and paragraph G (i.e. how the interpretation was revised).
Summarize the isolation experiments and what they established.
questions.a: Siffre spent two months underground without any means of telling time and emerged having undercounted the days, which was explained by an internal clock running slow without light to reset it. questions.a: The first result was real in its central claim and wrong in its numbers, and the corrections came from work that was possible only because the first result made the question seem worth asking.

note: A finding that is famous in its original form and has since been revised. Ask what the popular version still asserts and what the literature now says.

title: The Census That Burned
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The United States census of 1890 was taken, tabulated and published, and almost all of the original returns no longer exist. A fire in 1921 damaged the records, and what the fire did not destroy was largely disposed of some years later.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The loss is unusual among archival disasters because the scale is so complete. For most censuses a researcher can consult the original schedules and see individual households, and for 1890 that is impossible for all but a tiny fraction of the population.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What survives is the published statistical summary, which answers different questions entirely. A researcher can learn how many people lived in a county and how they were distributed by broad categories, and cannot learn who any of them were.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The gap falls in a place that makes it worse than its size suggests. The decades on either side were a period of very large migration into and within the country, and 1890 sits between two surveys that would otherwise allow households to be followed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Genealogical research is the most visible casualty and is not the most significant one. A family traceable through 1880 and 1900 can usually be bridged, and the missing decade is more damaging for people who moved, changed name or arrived during it, which is a particular population rather than a random sample.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The 1890 census is also the one that produced a famous administrative claim, which is now read differently because of the loss. Its superintendent observed that a frontier line could no longer be identified, and that observation became the basis of an influential thesis about American development.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Historians who later questioned that thesis wanted to re-examine the underlying returns, which is precisely what cannot be done. An argument built on a census is unusually difficult to evaluate when the census itself is gone.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode is why archival practice changed afterwards. Duplicate storage, dispersal of copies and formal retention schedules exist substantially because of losses like this one, and the 1890 census is the example invoked when the cost of not doing so has to be explained.

title: The Archive of Ordinary Days
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1937 a group in Britain began a project with an unusual premise. They proposed to record what ordinary people did and thought, on the grounds that nobody was recording it and that the newspapers purporting to represent public opinion were not evidence of it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The methods were deliberately plural and the plurality was the point. Volunteers kept diaries, observers recorded conversations in public places, and panels of correspondents answered open questions sent to them each month.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The directives are the richest of the three and the most unusual as evidence. A question such as what did you do yesterday evening, or what do you think about the news, produced hundreds of long answers from people with no reason to perform for anybody.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The material has obvious limitations that its own founders described. The volunteers were self-selected, they were disproportionately literate and left-leaning, and a person who agrees to write a monthly essay about their life is not typical of people in general.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What it captures that other sources do not is nevertheless substantial. Official records say what was decided, newspapers say what was said publicly, and these diaries say what somebody thought was worth mentioning about a Tuesday, which no other source preserves.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The project also captured changes of mind, which almost no historical source does. A diarist who held one view in 1938 and a different one in 1940 recorded both without knowing which would look better later, because the later view had not yet arrived.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It lapsed in the 1950s and was revived in 1981, and the revival produced a second difficulty of a different kind. Later volunteers knew the archive existed and knew they were writing for it, which changes what a diary is in a way that cannot be subtracted afterwards.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the collection supports a specific range of claims and not others. It is weak evidence about what people in general believed, strong evidence about how particular people reasoned, and unique evidence about what the texture of an ordinary day was understood to consist of.

title: The Experiment That Outlived Its Experimenters
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1927 a professor of physics at an Australian university heated a quantity of pitch, poured it into a sealed glass funnel, and allowed it to settle for three years before cutting the stem. The apparatus has been running ever since.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The purpose was demonstrative rather than investigative. Pitch at room temperature shatters when struck with a hammer, which is the behaviour of a solid, and the experiment was set up to show students that it is in fact an extremely viscous liquid.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The rate at which it behaves as one is the striking part. A drop forms over a period of years and detaches roughly once a decade, which means the entire visible result of a year's running is a very small change in the shape of a hanging blob of tar.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Fewer than ten drops have fallen in the whole period. The experiment has outlasted its originator, several custodians and the building it started in, and the intervals between drops have varied with temperature, particularly after air conditioning was installed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: For most of its existence nobody actually saw a drop fall. Drops were found to have fallen, which is a different thing, and the detachment itself went unobserved for more than eighty years through a sequence of near-misses that reads as comic.

paras.label: F
paras.text: One custodian stepped out for a cup of tea and missed one. A camera installed for the purpose malfunctioned at the critical moment on another occasion, and a drop fell during a period when the apparatus was unattended.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A fall was finally recorded on camera in 2013, not in Australia but at a similar experiment in Dublin that had been set up decades later and had attracted far less attention.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The experiment is often told as a joke and is a serious demonstration of something that is otherwise hard to convey. The distinction between a solid and a liquid is a matter of timescale, and the only way to show that is to pick a timescale longer than the patience of everyone involved.

title: The Animal Nobody Had Filmed
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The giant squid was known to science from carcasses for well over a century before anybody obtained an image of a living one. Specimens washed ashore on beaches, were taken up in fishing nets and were recovered from the stomachs of whales, and every single one of them was dead when it was examined.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That situation produced a strange kind of knowledge. The animal's anatomy was well described, its maximum size was argued about from measured specimens, and nothing whatever was known about how it moved, hunted or behaved.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The difficulty was a combination of depth and behaviour. The animal lives deep, the volume of ocean at those depths is enormous, and the methods available for exploring it were loud, bright and slow, which is a description of exactly what a deep-sea predator avoids.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The first photographs of a live animal were obtained in 2004 by a Japanese team using a baited line with a camera, which caught an individual attacking the bait at depth and recorded the sequence over several hours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The first video of one in its own environment followed in 2012, and the method that produced it is the interesting part. Rather than illuminating the animal, the team used a lure that imitated the bioluminescent display of a jellyfish under attack.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The reasoning behind that lure is worth stating because it is a piece of inference rather than engineering. A jellyfish displaying in that way is signalling to attract something large enough to attack whatever is attacking it, which makes the display an advertisement a predator has reason to investigate.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The camera system was also designed around the assumption that light drives the animal away. It used far red illumination, which the squid is believed not to see, so the recording is made in a wavelength outside the animal's own experience.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the result came from treating the failure as information. Decades of expeditions had established what does not work, and the successful method was built by assuming that every element of the standard approach was the reason for the standard outcome.
